description_full: MYR Group Inc., through its subsidiaries, provides electrical construction services in the United States and Canada. The company operates through two segments: Transmission and Distribution, and Commercial and Industrial. Its Transmission and Distribution segment offers a range of services on electric transmission and distribution networks, and substation facilities, including design, engineering, procurement, construction, upgrade, maintenance, and repair services with primary focus on construction, maintenance, and repair to customers in the electric utility industry; and services, including construction and maintenance of high voltage transmission lines, substations, and lower voltage underground and overhead distribution systems, clean energy projects, and electric vehicle charging infrastructure services, as well as emergency restoration services in response to hurricane, wildfire, ice storm, or other related damages. This segment serves as prime contractor to customers, such as investor-owned utilities, cooperatives, private developers, government-funded utilities, independent power producers, independent transmission companies, industrial facility owners, and other contractors. The Commercial and Industrial segment provides a range of services, including design, installation, maintenance, and repair of commercial and industrial wiring; and installation of intelligent transportation systems, roadway lighting, and signalization for airports, hospitals, data centers, hotels, stadiums, commercial and industrial facilities, clean energy projects, manufacturing plants, processing facilities, water/waste-water treatment facilities, mining facilities, intelligent transportation systems, roadway lighting, signalization, and electric vehicle charging infrastructure. This segment serves general contractors, commercial and industrial facility owners, governmental agencies, and developers. MYR Group Inc. was founded in 1891 and is headquartered in Thornton, Colorado.

financial_summary: MYR Group, Inc. is a mid-cap industrials business with a $4.1B market cap on $3.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +13% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 17% against a 10% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 12% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $232M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.76× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -12.7% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 30× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.8%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.4× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 5% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 39% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 26% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 48% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 51% and a beta of 1.11, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.41 vs 5y 1.17), so read it loosely.
About $74.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 49% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 64% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $250 (margin of safety -5%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 9%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $149 to $423 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/FCF 17.6 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 55% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.7% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $370 on average, 41% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 17% earns above the cost of capital of 10.2%, but the 7pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.36).
It runs a 12% gross margin and converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 2.76x, but high accruals (-12.7% of assets).
ROE of 18% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $91.1M (2% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.7, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.7% over 3 years, 10.2% over 5 years and 13.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 12%).
At current returns, reinvesting 23% of profits supports about 3.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 12.2% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.05, a backlog worth 69% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 7%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.4x, 2.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.9%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (18 sales, net $10.5M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.8% (1.8% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 1.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 9,000 employees, each generates about $406K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 11.7% a year.
That works out to $26K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.5M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
